data.text/markdown:
Tutorial 5: Catching flips in click records

Tutorial 4 monitored one small cat that we simulated ourselves. This tutorial takes a dataset of the challenge format and goes through the whole job of a flip detector once, on records where the physics can be seen by eye: the click records of a photon counter on the buffer output (the dataset tier A).
  • what a dataset of the challenge holds, and what a flip looks like in a record;
  • what a detector is, and how the leaderboard scores it;
  • three simple detectors, and a puzzle that the challenge asks you to solve.
Nothing in this tutorial is scored or handed in. The challenge asks for the same job on the heterodyne records (the dataset tier B), where the burst of a flip sits under the vacuum noise; the template notebook starts there. The click records stay available as a microscope for the physics questions of the challenge (steps 2 and 4). Times are in units of ||(1/\kappa_2||) (see docs/THEORY.md).

1. The dataset

A segment is one memory experiment: the cat is prepared in ||(|{+lpha} angle||), its buffer output is recorded for ||(T_{ m seg} = 200||), and the cat is read out. The label is 1 when the readout gave ||(-lpha||): the cat has flipped. Every split mixes segments of four cat sizes in random order, and the array nbar gives the cat size of each segment.
  • train: the nominal device, the one of the device sheet, which you can simulate;
  • val: the hidden test device, whose buffer has a finite bandwidth and whose memory has a small Kerr non-linearity. It is the device of the leaderboard.
records.load_dataset reads a split from the Aqora dataset, or from a file of that name if you put one in data/.

data.text/markdown:
Two trends run against each other, and they will matter in section 4: a bigger cat flips less often, and it clicks more often. Most clicks have nothing to do with a flip. A thermal photon or a dephasing event kicks the memory out of its code space for a moment, the buffer brings it back and sometimes emits a photon (tutorial 4, section 2), and the counter adds dark counts.

2. What a flip looks like

A record is a list of click times. Here are eight records with a flip label and eight without, at the largest cat size of the nominal device. The red bar marks the time unit of each record that holds the most clicks, and the number on the right counts them.

Most records with a flip label hold a tight cluster of clicks, a burst: the buffer radiates while the memory is out of its code space, and a flip is the longest excursion there is. The records without a flip label hold nothing of the kind, only the sparse clicks of the background. Zoom on a burst (change set_xlim) to see how long it lasts. Look again, though: not every record with a flip label shows a burst. Step 2 of the challenge asks why, and step 4 asks the mirror question, what a record with a burst and no flip label is.

3. A detector, and how it is scored

A detector takes the record and the cat size of a segment and returns a score: any real number, where higher means more suspicious. The crudest score is the total number of clicks of the segment. The leaderboard discards the 30 % of the segments with the highest scores, all cat sizes together, and compares the fraction of flips among the segments that are kept with the fraction of flips among all segments: ||[\rho_{70} = \frac{p_{\rm flip}(\text{kept segments})}{p_{\rm flip}(\text{all segments})}.||]It reports the flip suppression ||(1 - \rho_{70}||): 0 for scores that carry no information, 1 when every flip was discarded. scoring.rho_at_yield computes it on any labelled split, and scoring.postselection_curve gives ||(\rho||) for every yield (the fraction of segments kept).

data.text/markdown:
Discarding 30 % of the segments at random would remove 30 % of the flips and leave ||(\rho_{70} = 1||). The total count does a little better than chance, and not much.

4. Three detectors and a puzzle

Compare it with two others:
  • the cat size alone: discard the smallest cats first, without looking at any record. Small cats flip more often, so this is not as silly as it sounds;
  • the densest time unit: the largest number of clicks that a record holds within one time unit, the red bars of section 2 (tutorial 4 used the same idea).
The 30 % are one budget for the four cat sizes. scoring.by_cat_size shows where a detector spends it.

data.text/markdown:
Counting all the clicks of a record does worse than not looking at the records at all. Looking at the right place of the record, its densest time unit, beats both. Two remarks on the scores themselves. Both counts are integers, so hundreds to thousands of segments share the score at the 30 % cut, and the scorer ranks equal scores by their position in the file: a finer score breaks such ties better than chance. And the validation split is finite: with its 1257 flips, ||(1 - \rho_{70}||) is known to about ±0.02.

Questions

These are yours to think about; nothing here is handed in.
  1. Why does the total number of clicks lose to the cat size alone? The table of section 1 and the budget tables above hold the answer.
  2. The densest time unit ranks the records of one cat size well. Look at where it spends the budget across cat sizes: is that where the flips are? What would make the scores of a small cat and of a big cat comparable?
  3. The scores above are computed on the hidden device. Compute them on the nominal device (train) too. What changes, and what does not?
  4. Change the width of the window in burst_count. Which width works best, and what does it tell you about the duration of a burst?

From clicks to quadratures

The challenge is scored on the heterodyne records (dataset tier B): no clicks, but the two quadratures ||(I||) and ||(Q||) of the buffer output, averaged over 400 bins of half a time unit (tutorial 4, section 5). There a burst is a dip of ||(I||) of depth ||(\sqrt{2}\,\bar n||) that lasts about as long as the bursts above, under white noise of standard deviation 1.41 per bin: you will not see it by eye in a single record. The job is the same, a score for every segment and one budget for four cat sizes, and so is the puzzle. The template notebook 10_challenge_template.py takes over from here.
